levels.title: Name Finder
levels.story: Market Street is lined with shops, and every shop has a name over the door. Kit only knows the name of the one Farmer Juno has asked for. Where is it, on which road?

everyday.scene: You tell a taxi driver "the old bakery on Mill Road". The driver does not know the street number, so they ask a dispatcher, who asks the local council, until someone knows the exact address.
everyday.question: Would it make sense to keep one giant phone book that everyone in the world uses?
everyday.answer: It would be slow, hard to keep up to date, and one failure would stop everyone. Instead, different offices each look after their own part, and each knows who to point you to next. DNS works like that.

lessons.title: Names form a tree
text: People remember names, but machines route by numbers. The Domain Name System (DNS) turns names like www.juno-farm.example into addresses. A name reads from right to left, like a path down a tree.

Start at the invisible root. Below it sits the top-level domain (.example). Below that sits a domain (juno-farm) and then a subdomain (www). Each part of the tree is run by its own servers, called the authoritative servers for that zone. No single machine holds every name.

terms.meaning: The system that turns names into addresses.
The last part of a name, such as .org or .au.
The server that has the official answers for one zone.

predict.prompt: In www.juno-farm.example, which part sits closest to the root?
predict.answer: .example. Names read right to left, towards the root.

deeper.title: Why .example?
text: The top-level domain .example is reserved for examples and documentation, so it never points to a real site. That is why this game uses it for Juno's farm.

references.title: Peterson & Davie, Computer Networks: A Systems Approach, Infrastructure Services (DNS)
RFC 1034: Domain Names, Concepts and Facilities

lessons.title: Following the pointers
text: Your app does not walk the tree itself. It asks a local resolver, a server run by your network, to get the final answer. This is a recursive query: "do all the work and tell me the result".

The resolver then asks the tree, one step at a time. The root says "ask the .example servers". That server says "ask juno-farm.example's own server". That server finally gives the address. Each of these is an iterative query: "I do not know, but ask them".
The resolver keeps each answer for as long as its TTL (time to live) says, so repeat questions skip the walk.

terms.meaning: A server that looks names up on your behalf.
A question that says "get me the final answer".
A question that may be answered with "ask someone else".
How long an answer may be kept before it must be checked again.

predict.prompt: A resolver has just answered a lookup for www.juno-farm.example, with a TTL of 300 seconds. A minute later, someone asks again. Does it need to ask any servers?
predict.answer: No. The answer is still within its TTL, so it replies from its cache.

references.title: Peterson & Davie, Computer Networks: A Systems Approach, Infrastructure Services (DNS)
RFC 1034: Domain Names, Concepts and Facilities

lessons.title: What a name can hold
text: A DNS answer is a resource record: a name, a TTL, a type and a value. The type says what kind of fact it is.
Example: www.juno-farm.example, TTL 300, type A, value 203.0.113.80. DNS mostly runs over UDP, on port 53.

terms.meaning: One fact held in DNS, such as an address.

head: Type
Holds
rows: The mail server for a domain
The name server in charge of a zone
Plain text, often used to prove ownership

fieldNotes.title: Thirteen names, many machines
fieldNotes.text: There are 13 named root servers, but the root server system as a whole has more than 2,000 operating instances, run by 12 independent organisations. So the real number of machines is in the thousands, not 13.

summary: You followed a name down the DNS tree, saw which server answers which question, and watched a cache skip the whole walk.
A shopkeeper points down the street. "Number 80," she says. Kit has the address. But Moss is waiting at the door, and he wants to see what the web page looks like.

mistake.title: Thinking the root server knows every address
mistake.text: The root only knows who looks after each top-level domain. Each step along the way adds a little more detail, until the domain's own server gives the real answer.

levels.title: Web Waiter
levels.story: Mayor Moss runs the village website, and he checks it all day. The waiter at the Market Street café takes requests from customers and brings back pages, and sometimes bad news.

everyday.scene: At a café you ask the waiter for a coffee. They bring it, or say "sorry, we are out". The next time you order, they do not remember who you are.
everyday.question: If you want five things, is it quicker to walk to the counter five times, or to sit down and order them all?
everyday.answer: Sitting down is quicker. It saves the walk each time. Web connections work the same way: reusing one connection saves the cost of setting it up again.

lessons.title: Asking for a page
text: A web address, or URL, has parts: a protocol (https), a host (www.juno-farm.example) and a path (/menu/today). The browser looks up the host with DNS, opens a TCP connection to port 80, or 443 for secure HTTPS, and sends an HTTP request.
HTTP messages are plain text: a first line, some header lines, a blank line, and then the body. HTTP itself is stateless: each request stands alone, and the server does not remember earlier ones.

terms.meaning: A web address: protocol, host and path.
The language browsers and web servers use to ask and answer.
Forgetting each request as soon as it is answered.

lessons.diagramCaption: The shape of a request and a response.

predict.prompt: Which part of an HTTP message tells you whether the request worked?
predict.answer: The first line of the response, which holds the status code.

lessons.title: Verbs and verdicts
text: The first word of a request is a method. GET asks for a page. HEAD asks for only the headers. POST sends data, such as a form. PUT replaces something and DELETE removes it.

The response begins with a three-digit status code. The first digit gives the class: 2xx means success (200 OK), 3xx means go elsewhere or use your copy (301 Moved Permanently, 304 Not Modified), 4xx means the client made a mistake (403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found), and 5xx means the server failed (500, 503).

terms.meaning: The action a request asks for, such as GET.
A three-digit number that says how the request went.

lessons.diagramCaption: The five classes, by first digit (1xx is informational).

predict.prompt: A page that the server cannot find returns which code?
predict.answer: 404 Not Found, a client error: the request named something that is not there.

references.title: MDN Web Docs: HTTP response status codes
RFC 2324: Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol

lessons.title: Counting round trips
text: One round trip (RTT) is the time to send something and hear back. A web page is often a base page plus extras such as images. With non-persistent HTTP every object needs its own TCP connection: 1 RTT to set up and 1 RTT to fetch it, so 2 RTTs per object.

With a persistent connection, setup happens once, then each object costs 1 RTT. With pipelining, requests go out without waiting for each answer. Example: a base page plus 4 images is 10 RTTs non-persistent, 6 persistent, and 3 pipelined (setup, base page, then all 4 images at once).

terms.meaning: Round-trip time: send something and get a reply.
One TCP connection reused for many requests.
Sending several requests before the earlier answers arrive.

predict.prompt: A page has a base page and 6 images. Non-persistent HTTP, one object at a time. How many RTTs?
predict.answer: 14. There are 7 objects, and each takes 2 RTTs.

deeper.title: Sums are simplified
text: These counts ignore the time to push the bytes onto the link, and browsers also open several connections in parallel. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 send many requests at once over a single connection, giving the benefit of pipelining more safely.

references.title: MDN Web Docs: Connection management in HTTP/1.x

fieldNotes.title: A teapot that is not a joke
fieldNotes.text: There really is a status code 418, "I'm a teapot". It comes from an April Fools' joke document written in 1998 about controlling coffee pots over the web. Some servers still use it, mostly for fun.

source.title: Wikipedia: Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol

summary: You read the shape of an HTTP request, sorted status codes by their first digit, and counted round trips for three ways of fetching a page.
Moss refreshes the village page and smiles. "Number 80, there it is." But the envelope in Kit's satchel has acquired a stamp that was not there this morning. It is from someone Kit has never met.

mistake.title: Thinking 304 is an error
mistake.text: 304 Not Modified is not a failure. It tells the browser "your stored copy is still fine, use that", which saves downloading the page again.
